pos: n. (that which feeds a fire; rendering Hebrew ma'akoleth and oklah, both meaning food)
etymology: Old French fouaille, from Latin focus, a hearth. Both Hebrew words are the word for food: fuel is what the fire eats.
biblical_def: Isaiah of the day of the Prince of Peace: every battle of the warrior is with confused noise and garments rolled in blood, “but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire” (Isa 9:5); and of a people under wrath, “the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother” (Isa 9:19). Ezekiel's vine: “it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire devoureth both the ends of it, and the midst of it is burned. Is it meet for any work?” (Eze 15:4); “As the vine tree among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Eze 15:6). Of Ammon: “Thou shalt be for fuel to the fire” (Eze 21:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fuel as any matter which serves as aliment to fire; that which feeds fire; anything that serves to feed or increase flame, heat, or excitement.
webster_full: FUEL, n. Any matter which serves as aliment to fire; that which feeds fire; combustible matter, as wood, coal, peat, &c.
2. Any thing that serves to feed or increase flame, heat or excitement.
scriptures: Eze 15:4
Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire devoureth both the ends of it, and the midst of it is burned. Is it meet for any work?
Eze 15:6
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; As the vine tree among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
Isa 9:19
Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts is the land darkened, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother.
Thou shalt be for fuel to the fire; thy blood shall be in the midst of the land; thou shalt be no more remembered: for I the LORD have spoken it.
Isa 9:5
For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire.
corruption_summary: A church is valued for its size, and Ezekiel says a vine that bears no fruit is worth less than any tree of the forest, being good only for fuel.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 15 is a short chapter with one argument. The vine is the noblest plant in Scripture and the most useless as timber: you cannot make a pin of it to hang a vessel on, and when it has been through the fire once it is fit for nothing at all. Israel was the vine, and the vine's whole worth is its fruit; a fruitless vine is not a second-rate tree but a first-rate fuel. The church that has stopped bearing and comforts itself with its heritage should read verse 4 — is it meet for any work? — and the Lord's own word in John 15, where the branch that abideth not is cast into the fire. Isaiah 9:19 is the same fire on a people: as the fuel of the fire, no man sparing his brother, a society burning itself for warmth.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'akoleth (H3980), food, fuel; oklah (H402), food, what is eaten.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'akoleth (H3980) — fuel, what the fire eats; Isaiah 9:5, 9:19 only.
Hebrew oklah (H402) — food, fuel; Ezekiel 15:4, 15:6, 21:32, and of food generally, Genesis 1:29.
usage: “It is cast into the fire for fuel… Is it meet for any work?” — the fruitless vine.
“The people shall be as the fuel of the fire” — a society burning itself.
“Thou shalt be for fuel to the fire” — Ammon's sentence.

pos: v. (to feel one's way as a blind man; rendering Hebrew mashash and gashash)
etymology: Old English grāpian, to seize, feel. The Bible's gropers grope at noon — the blindness is in the man, not the hour.
biblical_def: The curse of the covenant: “thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness, and thou shalt not prosper in thy ways” (Deu 28:29). Isaiah's confession: “We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes: we stumble at noonday as in the night” (Isa 59:10). Of the crafty: “They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night” (Job 5:14). Of the counsellors God has made fools: “They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man” (Job 12:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grope as to feel along; to search or attempt to find something in the dark, or as a blind person, by feeling.
webster_full: GROPE, v.i. To feel along; to search or attempt to find something in the dark, or as a blind person, by feeling.
2. To seek blindly.
scriptures: And thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness, and thou shalt not prosper in thy ways: and thou shalt be only oppressed and spoiled evermore, and no man shall save thee.
We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes: we stumble at noonday as in the night; we are in desolate places as dead men.
Job 5:14
They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night.
They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man.
corruption_summary: A nation in full light and unable to find the wall is not unlucky; Deuteronomy calls it the curse.
corruption_paragraphs: Every verse that uses the word sets it at noon. The groping of Scripture is not the honest fumbling of a man in the dark; it is blindness in the daylight, and Deuteronomy 28:29 lists it among the curses of a covenant broken. A people with the light of the Word on every shelf and no ability to find the wall is under judgment, not under a cloud, and Isaiah 59:10 is the confession the judgment is meant to produce — we grope as if we had no eyes — spoken by the people themselves, with the reasons in the verses before: hands defiled with blood, lips speaking lies, feet running to evil. Job 12:25 adds the mechanism: He maketh them to stagger. Judicial blindness is God's act, and the only remedy is His also.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashash, piel (H4959), to grope, feel about; gashash (H1659), to feel with the hands, grope.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashash, piel (H4959) — to grope; Deuteronomy 28:29, Job 5:14, 12:25.
Hebrew gashash (H1659) — to grope, feel for; Isaiah 59:10 only.
usage: “Thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness” — the curse.
“We grope for the wall like the blind” — the confession the curse is for.
“They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger” — judicial blindness.

pos: n. and v. (armour; the gear of a war-horse; to arm, to yoke; rendering Hebrew shiryan, nesheq, and asar)
etymology: Old French harneis, gear, armour; the sense of horse-tackle came later. In Kings the harness is a coat of mail, and the joints of it are where the arrow went.
biblical_def: Ahab to Benhadad: “Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off” (1Ki 20:11). Of Ahab himself: “a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness” (1Ki 22:34; 2Ch 18:33). Jeremiah to Egypt: “Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets” (Jer 46:4). The kings brought Solomon “raiment, harness, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year” (2Ch 9:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines harness as armor, the whole accoutrements of a knight or horseman; the furniture of a draught horse; and, as a verb, to dress in armor, to equip.
webster_full: HARNESS, n. Armor; the whole accouterments or equipments of a knight or horseman.
2. The furniture of a draught horse, whether for a wagon, coach, gig, chaise, &c.
HARNESS, v.t. To dress in armor; to equip with armor for war.
2. To put on the furniture of a horse for draught.
scriptures: And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
And the king of Israel answered and said, Tell him, Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off.

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: therefore he said to his chariot man, Turn thine hand, that thou mayest carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
Jer 46:4
Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.
And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and raiment, harness, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year.
corruption_summary: The man who boasts before the battle has Ahab's own proverb against him, and Ahab's own harness had joints.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahab said the truest thing in his life to a drunken Syrian: let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off. Boasting belongs after the battle, if at all, and the man who announces the victory while buckling on the armour has Scripture's most worthless king for his authority. Two chapters later the same king put the harness on, disguised, against a prophecy, and a bow drawn at a venture found the joints of it. Every harness has joints; the coat of mail is a set of plates, and between the plates is where the arrow that has a man's name on it goes. Providence needs no aim. The doctrine of the verse is that there is no armour against a word from God, and the pastoral use of it is that there is no need of any other armour than the one Paul describes, which has no joints.
roots_summary: Hebrew shiryan (H8302), a coat of mail, harness; nesheq (H5402), weapons, armour; asar (H631), to bind, harness; chagar (H2296), to gird on.
roots_lines: Hebrew shiryan (H8302) — coat of mail, harness; 1 Kings 22:34, 2 Chronicles 18:33, 1 Samuel 17:5.
Hebrew chagar (H2296) — to gird on, of armour; 1 Kings 20:11; nesheq (H5402), armour; 2 Chronicles 9:24; asar (H631), to harness, bind; Jeremiah 46:4.
usage: “Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off” — Ahab's one true proverb.
“Between the joints of the harness” — providence needs no aim.
“Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen” — Egypt armed for Carchemish.

pos: n. pl. (cutting blades; at Gilgal, the flint knives of circumcision; rendering Hebrew chereb, ma'akeleth, and machalaph)
etymology: Old English cnīf. The knives of Joshua 5 are knives of flint — the old tool kept for the covenant sign after iron had come.
biblical_def: “At that time the LORD said unto Joshua, Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time” (Jos 5:2), “And Joshua made him sharp knives, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of the foreskins” (Jos 5:3). Baal's prophets on Carmel “cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them” (1Ki 18:28). Agur: “There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth” (Pro 30:14). Cyrus returned the temple vessels, among them “nine and twenty knives” (Ezr 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knife as a cutting instrument with a sharp edge or point, used for cutting food and for other purposes.
webster_full: KNIFE, n. plu. knives. A cutting instrument with a sharp edge or point, used for cutting food and for other purposes.
2. A sword or dagger.
scriptures: Jos 5:2
At that time the LORD said unto Joshua, Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time.
Jos 5:3
And Joshua made him sharp knives, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of the foreskins.
And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them.
There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men.
Ezr 1:9
And this is the number of them: thirty chargers of gold, a thousand chargers of silver, nine and twenty knives,
corruption_summary: The conquest is imagined beginning with a sword, and it began with knives, at Gilgal, on the wrong side of an army that could not march for days.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 5 is the least strategic chapter in the book. Israel had crossed Jordan into enemy country, Jericho was shut up before them, and the LORD's first command was not to attack but to make sharp knives and circumcise a generation born in the wilderness — disabling the whole army in the open for as long as it took to heal. The covenant sign came before the conquest, and the reproach of Egypt was rolled away at Gilgal before a wall fell. The church that wants the victories without the covenant, and the conquest without the cutting, has skipped the chapter the whole book depends on. Carmel's knives are the counterfeit: the prophets of Baal cutting themselves till the blood gushed, religion as self-harm to move a god who was not there, while Elijah's God answered a prayer of sixty words.
roots_summary: Hebrew chereb (H2719), a sword, a knife; ma'akeleth (H3979), a knife for eating or sacrifice; machalaph (H4252), a knife.
roots_lines: Hebrew charvot tsurim (H2719, H6697) — knives of flint; Joshua 5:2–3; chereb alone, 1 Kings 18:28.
Hebrew ma'akeleth (H3979) — knife; Proverbs 30:14, Genesis 22:6, 22:10; machalaph (H4252), Ezra 1:9.
usage: “Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again” — the covenant before the conquest.
“Cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets” — religion as self-harm.
“Their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor” — Agur's generation.

pos: v. (to pass the tongue over; of enemies, to lick the dust; rendering Hebrew laqaq and lachak, Greek apoleicho)
etymology: Old English liccian. The Bible's lickers are dogs at a king's blood, enemies at a King's feet, and the dogs at a beggar's sores.
biblical_def: Elijah to Ahab: “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine” (1Ki 21:19) — and they did (1Ki 22:38). Of the King: “They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him; and his enemies shall lick the dust” (Psa 72:9). Of Zion: “kings shall be thy nursing fathers… they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet” (Isa 49:23). Micah: “They shall lick the dust like a serpent” (Mic 7:17). Moab feared Israel would “lick up all that are round about us, as the ox licketh up the grass” (Num 22:4). And Lazarus: “the dogs came and licked his sores” (Luk 16:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lick as to pass or draw the tongue over the surface; to lap; to take in by the tongue.
webster_full: LICK, v.t. To pass or draw the tongue over the surface; as, a dog licks a wound.
2. To lap; to take in by the tongue; as, a dog or cat licks milk.
3. To lick up, to devour; to consume entirely.
scriptures: And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.
Psa 72:9
They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him; and his enemies shall lick the dust.

And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.
Mic 7:17
They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth: they shall be afraid of the LORD our God, and shall fear because of thee.
And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.
corruption_summary: The church expects to lick the dust before the kings of the earth, and Isaiah says the kings shall lick the dust of her feet.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 49:23 is a promise the timid church has never dared to believe. Kings shall be Zion's nursing fathers and queens her nursing mothers, and they shall bow with their faces to the earth and lick up the dust of her feet — not the church cringing before the state but the state on its face before the church, and the verse ends, thou shalt know that I am the LORD. Psalm 72:9 says the same of the King whose church it is: his enemies shall lick the dust. The pessimism that expects the gospel to lose is not humility; it is unbelief in a plain text. Naboth's vineyard is the word's other justice: the dogs licked the blood of the murdered man, and Elijah promised the same dogs the murderer's blood in the same place, and 1 Kings 22:38 records the licking with a clerk's precision. God's sentences are carried out to the letter of the sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew laqaq (H3952), to lap, lick; lachak (H3897), to lick, lick up; Greek apoleicho (G621), to lick off.
roots_lines: Hebrew laqaq (H3952) — to lick, lap; 1 Kings 21:19, 22:38, Judges 7:5.
Hebrew lachak (H3897) — to lick up; Psalm 72:9, Isaiah 49:23, Micah 7:17, Numbers 22:4.
Greek apoleicho (G621) — to lick; Luke 16:21 only.
usage: “Lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD” — kings before Zion.
“His enemies shall lick the dust” — the King of Psalm 72.
“Where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood” — carried out to the letter.

pos: n. (polished limestone; rendering Hebrew shayish and shesh, Greek marmaros)
etymology: Greek marmaros, from a root meaning to shine. The Hebrew shesh is also the word for fine white linen — both named for their whiteness.
biblical_def: David prepared for the house of God “marble stones in abundance” (1Ch 29:2). Ahasuerus's court had pillars of marble and “a pavement of red, and blue, and white, and black, marble” (Est 1:6). The bride of the Song: “His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars” (Sng 5:15). And among the merchandise no man buys any more in fallen Babylon: “all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble” (Rev 18:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marble as the popular name of any species of calcarious stone or mineral, of a compact texture, and of a beautiful appearance, susceptible of a good polish.
webster_full: MARBLE, n. The popular name of any species of calcarious stone or mineral, of a compact texture, and of a beautiful appearance, susceptible of a good polish.
2. A little ball of marble or other stone, used by children in play.
3. A stone remarkable for some inscription or sculpture.
scriptures: Sng 5:15
His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.

Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God the gold for things to be made of gold, and the silver for things of silver, and the brass for things of brass, the iron for things of iron, and wood for things of wood; onyx stones, and stones to be set, glistering stones, and of divers colours, and all manner of precious stones, and marble stones in abundance.
Est 1:6

Where were white, green, and blue, hangings, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble: the beds were of gold and silver, upon a pavement of red, and blue, and white, and black, marble.

The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble,
corruption_summary: The world's marble is Babylon's merchandise and Ahasuerus's pavement, and the church's marble is the legs of her Beloved.
corruption_paragraphs: Marble appears four times in Scripture and tells two stories. In Esther it is the pavement of a pagan king's drinking hall; in Revelation it is a line in the inventory of Babylon's trade, weeping merchants and no buyers. In Chronicles it is David's gift for the house of God, and in the Song it is the bride's description of her Beloved — his legs as pillars of marble set upon sockets of fine gold, strength standing on what is precious. The church has always read the Beloved as Christ, and the verse as her confession that He does not stagger: what bears the weight is stone, and what the stone stands on is gold. Babylon built with marble and it is gone; the bride described her Lord with it, and He stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew shayish (H7893) and shesh (H8336), white marble, alabaster; Greek marmaros (G3139), marble.
roots_lines: Hebrew shayish (H7893) — marble; 1 Chronicles 29:2; shesh (H8336), marble, and also fine linen; Song of Solomon 5:15, Esther 1:6.
Greek marmaros (G3139) — marble; Revelation 18:12 only.
usage: “His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold” — the Beloved does not stagger.
“Marble stones in abundance” — David's gift for the house.
“Brass, and iron, and marble” — Babylon's unsold inventory.

pos: v. (to move in military order; of God, to go forth before His people; rendering Hebrew tsa'ad and halak)
etymology: Old French marchier, to tread. The Hebrew of Psalm 68 and Habakkuk 3 is to step, to stride — the tread of God through the wilderness and the land.
biblical_def: “O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst march through the wilderness; Selah: The earth shook” (Psa 68:7–8). Habakkuk's prayer: “Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger” (Hab 3:12). Of the Chaldeans: “I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs” (Hab 1:6). Joel's locust army: “they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks” (Joe 2:7). Egypt's enemy “shall march with an army” (Jer 46:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines march as to move by steps and in order, as soldiers; to walk in a grave, deliberate, or stately manner; to move in military order.
webster_full: MARCH, v.i. To move by steps and in order, as soldiers; to move in a military manner.
2. To walk in a grave, deliberate or stately manner.
MARCH, n. The walk or movement of soldiers in order; a stately walk.
scriptures: Psa 68:7
O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst march through the wilderness; Selah:
Hab 3:12
Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.
Hab 1:6
For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs.
Joe 2:7
They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:
The voice thereof shall go like a serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood.
corruption_summary: God is said to be absent when a wicked nation marches, and Habakkuk was told that God raised the Chaldeans to march.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk's problem was not that God was absent from the Chaldean march but that He was behind it: I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land. The prophet asked how a holy God could use a nation worse than Judah to punish Judah, and he was not given an answer to the question but a vision of the end — the just shall live by his faith, and the Chaldean's turn would come. The doctrine is that every army that has ever marched has marched under a hand, and the prayer of chapter 3 is the prophet's peace with it: thou didst march through the land in indignation. Psalm 68 is the march the church sings: God going forth before His people through the wilderness, the earth shaking, Sinai moved — and Paul quotes the psalm of that march for the ascension of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsa'ad (H6805), to step, stride, march; halak (H1980), to go, walk, march.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsa'ad (H6805) — to step, march; Psalm 68:7, Habakkuk 3:12, Judges 5:4, 2 Samuel 6:13.
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, march; Habakkuk 1:6, Joel 2:7, Jeremiah 46:22.
usage: “When thou didst march through the wilderness” — God before His people, and the earth shaking.
“I raise up the Chaldeans… which shall march through the breadth of the land” — the army under a hand.
“Thou didst march through the land in indignation” — Habakkuk's peace with it.

pos: n. (one's trade or calling; rendering Hebrew ma'aseh and melakah, Greek techne)
etymology: Latin occupatio, a taking up; the work that takes up a man's time. In Genesis the word answers Pharaoh's question, and in Jonah the sailors'.
biblical_def: Joseph coached his brothers for Pharaoh's question: “when Pharaoh shall call you, and shall say, What is your occupation?” (Gen 46:33), and Pharaoh asked it: “What is your occupation? And they said unto Pharaoh, Thy servants are shepherds” (Gen 47:3). The sailors asked Jonah, “What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou?” (Jon 1:8). Paul at Corinth: “because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). Demetrius gathered “the workmen of like occupation” (Act 19:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines occupation as the act of taking possession; possession; that which engages the time and attention; the principal business of one's life; vocation; calling; trade.
webster_full: OCCUPATION, n. The act of taking possession.
2. Possession; a holding or keeping; tenure; use.
3. That which engages the time and attention; the principal business of one's life; vocation; calling; trade; the business which a man follows to procure a living or obtain wealth.
scriptures: Gen 47:3
And Pharaoh said unto his brethren, What is your occupation? And they said unto Pharaoh, Thy servants are shepherds, both we, and also our fathers.
Jon 1:8
Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?
Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
And it shall come to pass, when Pharaoh shall call you, and shall say, What is your occupation?
Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth.
corruption_summary: A trade is thought beneath a minister, and the apostle who wrote Romans made tents.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 18:3 records, without comment, that Paul made tents. He had been trained by Gamaliel, he had seen the risen Lord, and at Corinth he worked leather with Aquila and preached on the sabbath, and the church has spent centuries deciding whether that was a hardship or a principle. It was both, and it was not beneath him; the rabbis taught that a man who did not teach his son a trade taught him to steal. Genesis 47:3 is the older honesty: Jacob's sons told Pharaoh they were shepherds, an abomination to the Egyptians, because Joseph had told them to, and the despised occupation got them Goshen — a land apart, where they would not be absorbed. Jonah's occupation was prophet, and the sailors asked him what it was while he was running from it; the honest answer, I fear the LORD, was the beginning of his return.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639), work, deeds, occupation; melakah (H4399), business, occupation; Greek techne (G5078), a craft, trade.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639) — work, occupation; Genesis 46:33, 47:3; melakah (H4399), Jonah 1:8.
Greek techne (G5078) — a craft, trade; Acts 18:3, 17:29, Revelation 18:22; ergates (G2040), workmen; Acts 19:25.
usage: “By their occupation they were tentmakers” — the apostle who wrote Romans.
“What is your occupation? And they said unto Pharaoh, Thy servants are shepherds” — the despised trade that got them Goshen.
“What is thine occupation?” — asked of a prophet running from it.

pos: v. (set before, advanced in rank; rendering Greek emprosthen ginomai, Aramaic netsach, Hebrew shanah)
etymology: Latin praeferre, to carry before. The Baptist's Greek is literally that Christ has come to be in front of him — and then the reason, that He was before him.
biblical_def: John bare witness of Him: “This was he of whom I spake, He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me” (John 1:15); “He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose” (John 1:27); “After me cometh a man which is preferred before me: for he was before me” (John 1:30). Daniel “was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him” (Dan 6:3). Hegai “preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women” (Est 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preferred as regarded or valued more; advanced, as to an office or dignity.
webster_full: PREFERRED, pp. Regarded above others; elevated in estimation; chosen in preference to others; advanced to some office or dignity.
scriptures: John 1:15
John bare witness of him, and cried, saying, This was he of whom I spake, He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me.
John 1:30
This is he of whom I said, After me cometh a man which is preferred before me: for he was before me.
John 1:27
He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose.
Dan 6:3
Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.
Est 2:9

And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, which were meet to be given her, out of the king's house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women.
corruption_summary: The Baptist's for he was before me is passed over as a courtesy, and it is the pre-existence of the Son from the mouth of a man six months older than He.
corruption_paragraphs: John the Baptist was born six months before Jesus, and he said of Jesus, he was before me. The sentence is not deference; it is theology, and the fourth Gospel records it three times so that it cannot be missed. The One who came after John in time was before him in being, because He was in the beginning with God — the prologue of the same chapter — and the Baptist's reason for yielding first place was not that Jesus was greater but that He was earlier than the world. Every denial of the eternal Sonship has to get past a wilderness preacher who understood it. Daniel's preferment is the other kind: an exile advanced over the presidents of Persia because an excellent spirit was in him, and hated for it by men who could find no fault except in the law of his God.
roots_summary: Greek emprosthen mou gegonen (G1715, G1096), has come to be before me; Aramaic netsach (H5330), to distinguish oneself, be preferred; Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change, advance.
roots_lines: Greek emprosthen mou gegonen (G1715 with G1096) — is preferred before me; John 1:15, 1:27, 1:30.
Aramaic netsach, hithpael (H5330) — to be distinguished, preferred; Daniel 6:3; Hebrew shanah, piel (H8138), Esther 2:9.
usage: “Is preferred before me: for he was before me” — the eternal Son, from a man six months older.
“Whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose” — the greatest born of women on his knees.
“Daniel was preferred above the presidents” — an excellent spirit in an exile.

pos: n. (in the AV only in process of time, a course of days; rendering Hebrew miqqets yamim and yamim rabbim)
etymology: Latin processus, a going forward. The Authorized Version's phrase is the Hebrew at the end of days or after many days: the time it takes for a thing to come round.
biblical_def: “And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD” (Gen 4:3). “And it came to pass in process of time, that the king of Egypt died: and the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried” (Exo 2:23). “In process of time the daughter of Shuah Judah's wife died” (Gen 38:12). “In process of time, that the children of Ammon made war against Israel” (Jdg 11:4). And Jehoram's end: “in process of time, after the end of two years, his bowels fell out” (2Ch 21:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines process as a proceeding or moving forward; progressive course; course; continued series of actions or events; as, the process of time.
webster_full: PROCESS, n. A proceeding or moving forward; progressive course; tendency; as the process of man's understanding.
2. Proceedings; gradual progress; course; as the process of a war.
3. Operations; experiment; series of actions or experiments.
4. Course; continual flux or passage; as the process of time.
scriptures: Gen 4:3
And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD.
Exo 2:23

And it came to pass in process of time, that the king of Egypt died: and the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up unto God by reason of the bondage.
And in process of time the daughter of Shuah Judah's wife died; and Judah was comforted, and went up unto his sheepshearers to Timnath, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Jdg 11:4
And it came to pass in process of time, that the children of Ammon made war against Israel.

And it came to pass, that in process of time, after the end of two years, his bowels fell out by reason of his sickness: so he died of sore diseases. And his people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers.
corruption_summary: Process theology has a God who becomes in process of time, and Scripture's process of time is the unchanging God bringing His purposes round.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase belongs to providence. In process of time Cain brought an offering and the first murder followed; in process of time the king of Egypt died and Israel's groaning went up, and God remembered His covenant. Nothing in either verse hurried, and nothing was late. The theology that calls itself by the word has a different God — one who is Himself in process, developing with the world, learning from it, unable to guarantee an end — and it has taken the Bible's phrase for the slow unfolding of a fixed purpose and used it for a purpose that is not fixed. Exodus 2:23–25 is the rebuttal in four verbs: God heard, God remembered, God looked, God had respect. The process was in the days; the purpose was older than Egypt.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqqets yamim (H7093, H3117), at the end of days; yamim rabbim (H3117, H7227), many days; miyyamim, from days, after a time.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqqets yamim (H7093 with H3117) — at the end of days, in process of time; Genesis 4:3.
Hebrew bayyamim harabbim (H3117, H7227) — in those many days; Exodus 2:23; miyyamim, Judges 11:4; vayyirbu hayyamim, Genesis 38:12.
usage: “In process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground” — the first offering, and the first murder after it.
“In process of time, that the king of Egypt died” — nothing hurried, nothing late.
“In process of time, after the end of two years, his bowels fell out” — Jehoram's slow sentence.

pos: v. (in 1611 English, to fill; rendering Hebrew male, the ordinary word for fill)
etymology: Old French replenir, from Latin plenus, full. In the seventeenth century the word meant simply to fill, to stock; the sense of refill is later, and it has misled a theory.
biblical_def: The first blessing: “God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it” (Gen 1:28); and to Noah after the flood, in the same words, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth” (Gen 9:1). The Hebrew is the verb fill, used in the same chapter of the waters — “fill the waters in the seas” (Gen 1:22) — and elsewhere of Tyre “replenished” by the merchants of Zidon (Isa 23:2) and of God's promise, “I have replenished every sorrowful soul” (Jer 31:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines replenish as to fill; to stock with numbers or abundance; to finish, to complete; and, intransitively, to recover former fullness.
webster_full: REPLENISH, v.t. To fill; to stock with numbers or abundance. The magazines are replenished with corn. The springs are replenished with water.
2. To finish; to complete.
REPLENISH, v.i. To recover former fullness.
scriptures: Gen 1:28

And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
Gen 9:1
And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
Isa 23:2
Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle; thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished.
For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.
corruption_summary: The gap theory reads replenish as refill and finds a ruined world before Adam in it, and the Hebrew is the verb the same chapter uses for the fish.
corruption_paragraphs: The gap theory needed a text, and it found one in the English of 1611. If God told Adam to replenish the earth, the argument ran, the earth had been full before — a prior creation, ruined in a catastrophe between the first two verses of Genesis, with room in the gap for the ages of the geologists. The word will not carry it. In the translators' English replenish meant fill, as Webster still records; and the Hebrew is male, fill, the verb of Genesis 1:22 for the fish filling the seas, of Exodus 40:34 for the glory filling the tabernacle. The same command is given to Noah, whose earth had certainly been full before, in exactly the same words as to Adam, whose earth had not. A doctrine built on the drift of an English word is a doctrine built on nothing, and the mandate itself is the point: fill the earth, subdue it, have dominion — the first commission, never revoked.
roots_summary: Hebrew male (H4390), to fill, be full; ravah (H7301), to satiate, replenish.
roots_lines: Hebrew male, piel (H4390) — to fill, replenish; Genesis 1:28, 9:1, Isaiah 2:6, 23:2, Ezekiel 26:2, 27:25; and to fill, Genesis 1:22, Exodus 40:34.
Hebrew ravah (H7301) — to satiate, replenish; Jeremiah 31:25.
usage: “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it” — fill, in the translators' English.
“Replenish the earth” — to Noah, in the same words as to Adam.
“I have replenished every sorrowful soul” — the other filling.

pos: n. (harshness, severity in rule; rendering Hebrew perek)
etymology: Latin rigor, stiffness. The Hebrew perek occurs six times, and it is Egypt's word: the way Pharaoh made Israel serve.
biblical_def: “And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour: And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour” (Exo 1:13–14). Then the Law, three times: “Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour; but shalt fear thy God” (Lev 25:43); of the Israelite brother, “ye shall not rule one over another with rigour” (Lev 25:46); and of the man sold to a stranger, “the other shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight” (Lev 25:53).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rigor as stiffness; severity; sternness; strictness without allowance or abatement; hardness, austerity of life.
webster_full: RIGOR, n. Stiffness; rigidness.
2. Severity; sternness; strictness; as the rigor of criticism.
3. Severity of life; austerity; voluntary submission to pain, abstinence or mortification.
4. Strictness; exactness without allowance, latitude or indulgence; as the rigor of the law.
scriptures: Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour; but shalt fear thy God.
Exo 1:13
And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour:
Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.

And ye shall take them as an inheritance for your children after you, to inherit them for a possession; they shall be your bondmen for ever: but over your brethren the children of Israel, ye shall not rule one over another with rigour.
And as a yearly hired servant shall he be with him: and the other shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight.
corruption_summary: Scripture is charged with licensing slavery, and the Law forbade Israel the one thing Egypt had done to her, with the fear of God as the reason.
corruption_paragraphs: The Law of the servant in Leviticus 25 is written by the survivors of Egypt, and it uses Egypt's word. Israel had served with rigour; therefore Israel shall not rule with rigour, and the reason given is not sentiment but theology: but shalt fear thy God. The master's restraint is grounded in his own Master, and the third occurrence adds in thy sight — the Israelite is responsible for what a stranger does to his brother where he can see it. The charge that the Bible endorses the slave trade has to be made against a code that made kidnapping a capital crime (Exo 21:16), freed the servant in the seventh year with a gift, and forbade rigour by name. What the Law regulated, it regulated toward the exodus; what the traders did, the Law had already called Egypt.
roots_lines: Hebrew perek (H6531) — rigour, harshness; Exodus 1:13–14, Leviticus 25:43, 25:46, 25:53, Ezekiel 34:4.
usage: “All their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour” — Egypt's word.
“Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour; but shalt fear thy God” — the master's Master.
“Shall not rule with rigour over him in thy sight” — responsible for what you can see.
